The environment is crucial to the evaluation process, because it determines the context in which an expression should be evaluated. Indeed, one could say that expressions in a programming language do not, in themselves, have any meaning. Rather, an expression acquires a meaning only with respect to some environment in which it is evaluated.
Even the interpretation of an expression as straightforward as (+11) depends on an understanding that one is operating in a context in which + is the symbol for addition.
Even the interpretation of an expression as straightforward as display(1) depends on an understanding that one is operating in a context in which the name display refers to the primitive function that displays a value.
Thus, in our model of evaluation we will always speak of evaluating an expression with respect to some environment. To describe interactions with the interpreter, we will suppose that there is a global environment global environment, consisting of a single frame (with no enclosing environment) that includes values for the
